session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

masculine_norms.construct: Traditional masculinity norms measured with the Male Role Norms Inventory (MRNI; Levant et al., 1992), subscales: avoidance of femininity, restrictive emotionality, aggression, achievement status, self-reliance, and attitudes toward sex (54 items; homophobia subscale excluded).
masculine_norms.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger endorsement of traditional masculine norms.

masculinity_of_meat.construct: Perceived masculinity of meat measured with the 7-item Masculinity of Meat scale (Lax & Mertig, 2020; e.g. 'Men need to eat meat more than women do').
masculinity_of_meat.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger perceived masculinity-meat link and anti-vegetarian bias.

meat_attachment.construct: Meat attachment measured with a 5-item shortened form of the Meat Attachment Questionnaire (Graca et al., 2015; e.g. 'Meat is irreplaceable in my diet').
meat_attachment.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger emotional and habitual attachment to eating meat.

dairy_attachment.construct: Dairy attachment measured on an identical scale to meat attachment, with 'dairy' replacing 'meat' (Graca et al., 2015 adaptation).
dairy_attachment.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger emotional and habitual attachment to dairy consumption.

vegetarianism_threat.construct: Perceived threat from the rise of vegetarianism measured with the 8-item Vegetarianism Threat Scale (Dhont & Hodson, 2014; e.g. 'The rise of vegetarianism poses a threat to our country s cultural customs').
vegetarianism_threat.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger perceived societal or cultural threat from vegetarianism.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This introductions section surfaced an early thematic tension between rurality and urban life as frameworks for understanding food attitudes — specifically whether proximity to food production (knowing farms, local meat) creates a meaningfully different relationship to eating than anonymous supermarket consumption. Participants broadly accepted the rural/urban distinction as real but resisted any implied hierarchy between the two, with the urban participants asserting equivalence rather than deficit.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main move was keeping introductions functional while letting an organically emerging theme (rural vs. urban food connection) breathe briefly before redirecting. Drawing David in by direct address after he'd stayed quiet worked — he added useful complexity rather than just agreeing. The redirect to the next section felt clean given the thread had reached a natural pause. Risk was letting it run slightly long, but the thematic payoff justified it.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. We're going to spend about 45 minutes just having a conversation about your food choices and opinions, and I should let you know the session is being recorded for research purposes. Before we get going, a few quick things: there genuinely are no right or wrong answers here — I'm not testing you on anything, I'm just interested in what you actually think and do. So try not to overthink it, just speak freely. And this is meant to be a conversation, not an interview — so if something comes up and you want to jump in or respond to what someone else has said, please do. You don't have to wait for me to call on you. The only thing I'd ask is that we're respectful of each other and try to keep things fairly brief so everyone gets a chance to speak. Okay — let's start simple. If you could just go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that'd be great.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham — West Midlands. Twenty years old. Yeah, that's me really.
Yeah, I'm Ibrahim. I'm from up here in the North East — urban area. I'm 24. Been living here for a while now, so... yeah, that's me.
Right, I'm Will. I'm from a village in Scotland — properly rural, so quite different from what you lot are describing I reckon. I'm 29. That's about it really.

Right, yeah, I'm Isaiah — I'm from Yorkshire, urban area like Ibrahim. I'm 26. 

And actually that's interesting what you said, Will — about rural being different. I was just thinking, like, do you reckon that actually shapes what people eat? Because I've got mates whose families are from the countryside and they seem to have totally different attitudes to food, but I'm not sure if that's just them being different people or if it's actually a location thing. What's the difference you're thinking of?

Yeah, it's a fair question. I mean, for one thing the shops are just different out here — you've got maybe one supermarket within reasonable distance, so you make do with what's there. But it's more than that really. There's a lot of farming around where I am, so meat especially... it's not abstract, you know? You know the farms, you might know the people, there's a sense of it being local. That shapes how people think about it.

And family stuff too — my old man, his dad farmed, so there's always been this thing around proper meals with meat in them. It's just normal. I'm not saying it's better or worse than what you lot do, but it's definitely different culturally. In a village, food's more tied to... tradition, I suppose, and what's actually available rather than what you're choosing from twenty options.

That's a really interesting distinction, Will — the idea that food being less abstract, more tied to place and people you actually know, shapes how you think about it. David, we haven't heard from you yet — where are you joining us from?

I'm David, from Glasgow actually — urban Scotland like Will but obviously pretty different from a village setup. I'm 27.

But yeah, what you're saying about it being less abstract — I think that's interesting. I mean, I do eat meat fairly regularly, but I don't have that same kind of... connection to it, I suppose. It's just what I buy from the shop. I don't think about the farms or any of that really. 

I wonder though if that difference you're describing — between knowing where it comes from and just picking it off the shelf — I'm not sure that automatically makes people think differently about it in a good way or a bad way. Like, Will's saying it's tradition and local, which fair enough, but I don't think not having that connection means people in cities are doing something weird. It's just a different way of living, isn't it?

Cheers, David — and yeah, that urban versus rural thing is an interesting thread we can come back to. Right, so we've all got a sense of where everyone's coming from. Let's move on a bit. Thinking about the places you spend time with your male friends — where do you actually go? Like, if you had a favourite spot in your city or town for hanging out with your mates, what would it be, and why that place?

Yeah, so for me it's usually the pub, to be honest. There's a few decent ones near where I am — you've got your standard chain places but also some proper local spots where everyone kind of knows each other. That's where you end up most weekends with the lads. 

There's also the football — go watch matches when there's something on, grab a pint after. That's a big thing for us up here. And then just, you know, different restaurants and that depending on what mood you're in. Sometimes it's a curry, sometimes you'll go for a burger place. Nothing mad really, just the normal spots you'd find in any city I reckon.

I mean, the pub's probably the main one though. That's where you actually spend time talking to people properly, isn't it, rather than just being somewhere to eat.

Yeah, I'd say it's pretty similar down here in Birmingham actually. The pub's definitely where you end up with your mates — that's just where you go, innit. There's loads of them around, and you've got your regulars where people know you. 

And like, you're right about the restaurants too, Ibrahim. You kind of pick depending on what you're feeling — curry, burger, pizza, whatever. But I think that's actually where you notice what people are eating, you know? Like, you're out with the lads and someone's ordering something different, or mentioning they don't eat meat or whatever, and that's when it comes up in conversation. It's not something you'd normally talk about just sitting around, but when you're actually choosing food together it becomes a thing.

The pub though, yeah — that's the main spot where actual conversation happens.
